subject: Clarify proration, quarterly true-up and make-good mechanics for hosted volume commit
messages:

Subject: Clarify commit true-up / proration rules for Hosted API

Marcus —

Thanks again for the demo. Procurement and finance at Acme want to explicitly understand how Redwood handles: mid-term commit increases/decreases, quarterly true-ups vs an annual reconciliation, and what you call make-goods / credits when actual usage misses the commit. Can you confirm:

- If we add or reduce committed tokens mid-quarter, how do you prorate discounts?
- Do quarterly true-ups happen as credits/invoices in the month after quarter close?
- At year end do you do a single annual true-up that supersedes quarter adjustments?
- If we underuse vs committed, is the shortfall automatically credited, carried forward, or invoiced as a make-good? Any limits?

We'd appreciate a simple example invoice timeline and one or two worked numeric examples (small and large).

Also attaching our internal procurement checklist; happy to jump on a quick call next week.

Hi Sam —

Thanks — great set of questions. High level answer first, then I'll loop in Finance & Legal for firm contractual language and a short playbook. TL;DR: we support mid-term prorations, quarterly true-ups for usage vs commit (adjustments billed the month after quarter close), and an annual reconciliation that finalizes any outstanding make-goods/credits for the contract year.

Key bullets:
- Mid-term changes: increases apply immediately and discounts are prorated for the remaining billing period; decreases require 30 days' notice and are prorated at the time of change (we avoid retroactive positive credits for decreases except in limited negotiated cases).
- Quarterly true-up: we compare billed commit to actual billed usage by token; if usage > commit, you'll be invoiced for overage at the committed unit price tier (or standard overage rate if you exceed top tier). If usage < commit, we first apply any available credits (from prior make-goods), then carry a credit forward; the contract defines whether that shortfall is a refundable credit or a non-refundable make-good credit — typical enterprise SOWs offer a one-year carry-forward credit, with year-end reconciliation adjusting permanent shortfalls.
- Annual reconciliation: performed within 30 days after contract year end to settle any residual shortfall or overage and produce a final invoice/credit for the contract year.

I'm attaching a quick workbook with scenarios; Monica, can you and Neha confirm the standard Redwood stance on carry-forward window and the exact billing timeline? We'll follow with a one-pager for Acme.

Thanks,
Marcus

Marcus / Neha —

See proposed canonical text below plus an annotated example. This is our default enterprise posture; we can negotiate different carry-forward windows or refundability on a per-deal basis.

Canonical wording (SOW language, suggested):
"Committed token volumes are purchased per contract year and billed monthly. Customers may request changes to committed volumes with 30 days' written notice. Mid-term increases in committed volume go into effect immediately and are prorated for the remainder of the billing period. Mid-term decreases require 30 days' notice and are prorated from the effective date onward; Redwood does not provide retroactive refunds for decreases except as explicitly negotiated.

Quarterly True-up: Within 30 days following each calendar quarter close Redwood will perform a usage reconciliation comparing actual billable token usage to committed volumes. Any overage will be invoiced at the agreed committed unit price or the applicable overage rate, whichever is lower. Any net shortfall (committed > actual) will be treated as a make-good credit and applied to future invoices for up to twelve (12) months from the date of the shortfall, unless otherwise agreed.

Annual Reconciliation: Within 30 days after the end of the contract year Redwood will perform a final reconciliation. Residual shortfalls not consumed as carry-forward credits during the contract year will be invoiced as a final make-good at the contracted unit price unless the parties agree to a different treatment in the SOW.
"

Annotated example (numbers simplified):
- Contract year commit: 6B tokens (500M/month average). Tiered discount applies starting at 1B tokens/month.
- Q1 actual: 400M/month (1.2B quarter) — result: shortfall vs quarterly expected 1.5B = 300M tokens. We create a 300M-token credit applied to future invoices; it expires 12 months after issuance unless used.
- Q2 actual: 600M/month (1.8B quarter) — overage relative to committed monthly average billed at contracted per-token price for incremental usage; will be invoiced in month after quarter close. Credits from Q1 offset part/all of Q2 overage if present.
- Mid-year increase: Acme increases commit by 20% mid-May. Increase is prorated for remainder of June onward; invoices reflect new discounted unit price applied to tokens after effective date. Decreases: not retroactively refunded.

Billing timeline (suggested language):
- Invoices issued monthly for that month's usage and committed charges.
- Quarterly true-up adjustments (credit or invoice) issued in the month following quarter close (e.g., Q1 true-up issued in April).
- Annual reconciliation adjustments issued within 30 days after contract year end.

Operational notes / edge cases:
- We can optionally include an automatic rollover of credits across contract years for multi-year SOWs if the customer wants that; by default credits expire 12 months from issuance.
- For very large make-goods (e.g., >20% of annual commit) Finance prefers a two-step settlement (apply credits first, then issue a final invoice at annual reconciliation) to avoid large negative invoices mid-year.

I can turn this into a one-page handout for Sam and the procurement team. Neha, please confirm revenue recognition implications and whether Finance wants a different expiration for credits.

—Monica

Sam —

Thanks for the questions. Below is the concise playbook and some concrete timelines we use by default. I've attached a one-pager and the scenario workbook for your team.

Short playbook (for procurement SOW language):
1) Billing cadence: Monthly invoices for actual usage + committed reservation charges.
2) Mid-term modifications: 30 days' notice for decreases; increases effective immediately and prorated.
3) Quarterly true-up: Reconciliation performed within 30 days of quarter close. Overages invoiced, shortfalls issued as make-good credits (12-month expiry).
4) Annual reconciliation: Final settlement within 30 days after contract year; any residual shortfall may be invoiced as final make-good unless otherwise agreed.

Example timelines:
- Q1 true-up issued in April; Q2 in July; annual reconciliation in January (for a calendar-year contract).
- Credits are visible on monthly invoices and applied automatically against new invoices until consumed or expired.

Next steps:
